q: n ≤ 2·10⁵, time limit 1 to 2 s. Which complexity should your solution aim for?
w: O(n²) is 4·10¹⁰ steps, far too slow. n log n is about 3.5·10⁶.

q: n ≤ 20. Which brute force is usually fine?
o: Try every pair of subsets: O(4ⁿ)

q: n ≤ 8. You want to try every ordering of the elements. How many orderings is that?
n ≤ 500. Which complexity is the setter most likely expecting?
w: 500³ = 1.25·10⁸: fine in C++, tight in Python. A small cap like this hints that n³ is allowed.

q: n ≤ 5000. Which complexity is the setter most likely expecting?
w: 5000² = 2.5·10⁷. A cap of a few thousand usually signals quadratic, like an O(n·m) DP.

q: The input is a single number n ≤ 10¹⁸. What should your solution look like?
w: Even √(10¹⁸) = 10⁹ is too many steps. Look for a formula, binary search, or fast exponentiation.

q: Array of 2·10⁵ numbers and 2·10⁵ queries "sum of a[l..r]", no updates. Best approach?
o: Loop from l to r for each query
w: Build pre once in O(n); each answer is pre[r] − pre[l−1]. Looping per query is up to 4·10¹⁰ steps.

q: t ≤ 10⁴ test cases, sum of n ≤ 2·10⁵. Each test runs cnt = [0] * (2*10**5 + 1). What happens?
o: Fine, because the sum of n is small
w: Reset cost must scale with that test’s n, not the global max. Allocate size n + 1 or clear only what you touched.

q: n ≤ 40. Find a subset with sum exactly S (values up to 10¹⁸). Best approach?
o: Meet in the middle: enumerate each half of 20
w: 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ sums per half. Sort one side, then binary search or hash for S − x. DP over a sum this big is impossible.

q: Roughly how big is 2²⁰?
w: 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³, so 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ and 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹. Use this to size a brute force in seconds.

q: How many steps does binary search need over the range 1 to 10⁹?
w: log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30. Binary search on the answer is cheap even with an O(n) check per step.

q: n = 2·10⁵. How many pairs (i, j) with i < j exist?
w: n(n − 1)/2 ≈ 2·10¹⁰. Problems about pairs at this size need counting tricks (sorting, hashing, two pointers), not enumeration.

q: A 1000 × 1000 grid. Is a BFS over all cells feasible?
o: Only if the grid is a tree
w: BFS is O(cells + edges) ≈ 5·10⁶. In Python, use a deque and flat arrays.

q: n ≤ 10¹². You need to test whether n is prime, once. Is trial division up to √n OK?
o: Only with a sieve up to 10¹²
w: Trial division stops at √n, so 10⁶ iterations. Many such queries would change the answer.

q: The most divisors any n ≤ 10⁹ can have is about…
w: Highly composite numbers below 10⁹ top out at 1,344 divisors. Looping over all divisors of a number is cheap.

q: Rough CPython speed for simple loop operations per second?
w: CPython does roughly 10⁷ simple operations per second; PyPy and C++ are much faster. Budget your brute force with this.

q: The Sieve of Eratosthenes up to N runs in…
w: Each composite is crossed out once per prime factor, which totals N log log N, nearly linear.

q: Which loop visits every subset of n items as a bitmask?
w: 1 << n is 2ⁿ. Item i is in the subset when (mask >> i) & 1 is 1.

q: Inside the mask loop, how do you test whether item i is chosen?
w: Shift bit i down to position 0, then keep only that bit. In Python, >> binds tighter than &, so no parentheses are needed.

q: len(list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=n))) equals…
w: product with repeat=n builds every length-n tuple over {0, 1}: one tuple per subset.

q: How many tuples does itertools.combinations(range(5), 2) produce?
w: C(5, 2) = 10. permutations(range(5), 2) would give 20, because order matters there.

q: Count pairs (x, y) with x + y = S and 1 ≤ x, y ≤ 10⁶. Fastest brute force?
o: Loop x, set y = S − x, check its range
Two nested loops over x and y
w: Fix one variable and the other is forced: O(10⁶) instead of O(10¹²). "Fix one, derive the rest" rescues many brute forces.

q: Find a, b, c ≥ 0 with a + b + c = n and some condition, n ≤ 3000. Good loop plan?
o: Loop a and b, set c = n − a − b
Loop over all triples up to n³
w: Two loops and the third value is determined: about 9·10⁶ instead of 2.7·10¹⁰.

q: Your greedy gets WA on test 3 and you can’t see why. Best next move?
o: Write a brute force, run both on small random tests, compare
Add prints to the greedy only
w: Stress testing finds a tiny counterexample fast. Keep n between 1 and 6 so the brute force is instant and the failing case is readable.

q: A problem asks for f(n) with n ≤ 10¹⁸. Good first move in a contest?
o: Brute force f(n) for n = 1..15 and look for a pattern
w: Small cases often reveal a formula or a repeating cycle. Print a table, spot the rule, then verify it on more values.

q: Looping over all submasks of every mask of n bits (sub = (sub − 1) & mask) costs in total…
w: Each bit is outside the mask, in the mask only, or in both: three choices per bit. n = 15 gives about 1.4·10⁷.

q: Count the 1 bits in mask (Python 3.10+)?
w: On older judges use bin(mask).count("1"). bit_length() gives the position of the highest bit, not the count.

q: The answer k is guaranteed to be between 1 and 60, and checking one k is O(n). Simplest plan?
o: Try every k from 1 to 60, take the first that works
w: 60 × O(n) is cheap. When the answer space is tiny, brute forcing over answers beats being clever.

q: A grid has n·m ≤ 2·10⁵, but n or m alone can be 2·10⁵. Your idea costs O(min(n,m)² · max(n,m)). Safe?
w: min(n, m) ≤ √(2·10⁵) ≈ 447, so the total is about 9·10⁷. Transposing so the short side comes first is a classic trick. Tight in Python.

q: To list all divisors of n efficiently, loop i from 1 while…
o: i * i <= n, adding i and n // i
i * i < n, adding only i
w: Divisors come in pairs (i, n/i). Stop at √n and add both, but don’t add i twice when i * i == n.

q: A string of length n. How many substrings, and what does slicing all of them cost?
w: Each slice costs up to O(n). Fine for n ≤ 300; past that, think hashing or a smarter scan.

q: Every string of length n over an alphabet of size k. How many are there?
w: Each of n positions has k choices. 26⁴ ≈ 4.6·10⁵ is fine; 26⁶ ≈ 3·10⁸ is not.

q: Find i < j < k with a[i] + a[j] + a[k] = 0, n ≤ 3000. Best plan?
o: Sort, fix i, two pointers for j and k: O(n²)
w: 3000³ = 2.7·10¹⁰ is too slow. Fixing one index and sweeping two pointers on the sorted rest is about 9·10⁶.

q: Brute force over all permutations of n ≤ 9 elements with an O(n) check each. Total work?
w: 9! · 9 ≈ 3.3·10⁶, fine even in Python. n = 11 would be about 4.4·10⁸, too slow.

q: "Max difference between adjacent elements", and n can be 1. What’s the risk?
o: No adjacent pairs exist, so max() of an empty list crashes
w: Always try n = 1 (and n = 0 if allowed). Check what the statement wants printed in that case.

q: (-7) % 3 in Python gives…
w: Python’s % takes the sign of the divisor, so the result is in [0, 3). C++ gives −1, so there you add MOD before taking %.

q: -7 // 2 in Python gives…
w: // floors toward −infinity. C++ / truncates toward zero and gives −3. This bites with negative midpoints and when porting code.

q: In C++, 2·10⁵ values each up to 10⁹ are summed into an int. What happens?
o: Overflow: the sum can reach 2·10¹⁴, use long long
It only fails with negative values
w: int caps near 2.1·10⁹. Python ints never overflow, which is a good reason to stay in Python when numbers get big.

q: Multiple test cases, and you forget to reset a global counter. Symptom?
o: Test 1 passes, later tests are wrong
w: Samples often have one case, so this only shows on the judge. Reinitialize per test, or put each test in a function.

q: A tree with n nodes is given as n − 1 edges. Which n breaks careless input code?
o: n = 1: there are zero edge lines
w: With n = 1 there is nothing to read, and code that assumes node 2 exists breaks. Also test a tree that is one long path.

q: Sorted list with duplicates. First index where a[i] ≥ x?
w: bisect_left lands on the first copy of x. bisect_right lands just after the last copy.

q: for i in range(1, n): visits which values?
w: range stops before its end. For a 1-indexed loop through n, write range(1, n + 1).

q: Count pairs i < j with a[i] == a[j]. A value appears c times. How many pairs does it add?
w: Choose 2 of its c positions. c² counts ordered pairs and i = j.

q: Counting connected components, you BFS only from node 1. What breaks?
o: Nodes not reachable from 1 are never counted
w: Loop over every node and start a new BFS from each unvisited one. Disconnected graphs are a favorite hidden test.

q: Input says 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹ operations. Which k do people forget?
w: With k = 0 the answer is usually the input as is. Code that does one step first and repeats k − 1 times breaks here.

q: Checking that an array is strictly increasing. Which test catches a ≤ vs < bug?
w: Strict means equal values fail. Equal elements are the boundary, so always test them.

q: Circular array of n elements. The right neighbor of the last index n − 1 is…
w: Use % n to wrap around, or append the array to itself (a + a) to turn circular windows into normal ones.

q: Intervals [l, r] are inclusive. Do [1, 3] and [3, 5] overlap?
o: It depends on the sort order
w: With inclusive endpoints, touching is overlapping. Closed vs half-open intervals flips your comparison, so read the statement.

q: print(*arr) when arr is empty prints…
w: print() with no arguments still prints a newline. Check whether the problem expects a count line or −1 instead.

q: Sorted list a of even length n (0-indexed). The usual median is…
w: Even length has two middle values. Many problems define "median" as the lower or upper one, so read the definition.

q: int(10**18 / 3) compared with 10**18 // 3 in Python?
o: The first can be off: / makes a float with 53 bits of precision
w: Floats hold about 15 to 16 significant digits. Keep big integer math in ints with //, and use math.isqrt, not int(math.sqrt(x)).

q: "If impossible, print −1." What do people miss most often?
o: Detecting impossibility, so an unreached INF gets printed
w: Keep a flag or a sentinel like INF, and check it before printing. Printing a leftover 10¹⁸ distance is a classic WA.

q: A grid is 1 × m. Which bug does that test catch?
o: Code that assumes at least 2 rows, like reading grid[1]
w: Thin grids (1 × m, n × 1, 1 × 1) break neighbor logic and corner handling. Always try them.

q: Why test a string where every character is the same, like "aaaa"?
o: It maximizes matches, exposing counting bugs and worst-case time
w: Uniform strings are the worst case for many substring loops and break code that assumes distinct characters.

q: Find i ≠ j with a[i] + a[j] = x using a set of all values. What breaks?
o: x = 2v where v appears once: v pairs with itself
w: Use a count map, or check the set before adding the current element, so an element can’t pair with itself.

q: Fastest common way to read a lot of input in Python?
o: sys.stdin.readline, or read everything with sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
w: input() is noticeably slower past 10⁵ lines. Alias input = sys.stdin.readline and .strip() any strings.

q: Printing 2·10⁵ answers with one print() each is slow. Better?
w: One large write is much faster than many small ones.

q: Recursive DFS on a path of 2·10⁵ nodes in Python. Most likely result?
o: RecursionError, or a crash from stack overflow
w: The default recursion limit is about 1000, and raising it can still overflow the C stack. Write DFS with your own stack.

q: grid = [[0] * m] * n, then grid[0][0] = 1. What happens?
w: * n repeats one inner list n times. Use [[0] * m for _ in range(n)].

q: q.pop(0) on a list of 10⁵ items, done 10⁵ times. Cost?
o: O(n²) overall: each pop shifts the list
w: Use collections.deque and popleft() for BFS queues; it is O(1).

q: You check "x in arr" 10⁵ times on a list of 10⁵ items. Fix?
o: Turn arr into a set first
w: Membership is O(n) in a list and O(1) on average in a set.

q: Which kind of heap does heapq give you?
w: For a max-heap push −x and negate on pop. For pairs, push (−priority, item).

q: a = input().split(); a.sort() with input "10 9 100". Result?
w: They are strings, so they sort as text. Convert first: list(map(int, input().split())).

q: Sort points by y descending, then x ascending. Which key?
w: Tuple keys compare left to right. reverse=True would also flip the x order.

q: round(2.5) in Python 3 returns…
w: Python rounds half to even. For normal rounding of non-negative values use int(x + 0.5), or better, stay in integers.

q: b = a for lists, then b.append(5). What happens to a?
o: a also gets 5: both names point to one list
w: Use b = a[:] or a.copy() for a shallow copy (copy.deepcopy for nested lists).

q: Modular inverse of a mod a prime p in Python 3.8+?
w: pow(a, -1, p) works whenever a and p are coprime. Fermat’s pow(a, p − 2, p) also works for prime p.

q: Fast way to compute aᵇ mod m with b up to 10¹⁸?
o: Multiply in a loop b times
w: Three-argument pow runs in O(log b). a ** b builds an astronomically large number first.

q: Your Python loops 10⁷ times and gets TLE on Codeforces. First thing to try?
o: Submit with PyPy instead of CPython
w: PyPy compiles hot loops, often 5 to 20 times faster. The exception is deep recursion, which is worse on PyPy.

q: Why wrap a Python solution in def main(): and then call main()?
o: Local variable access is faster than global access
w: In CPython, locals are looked up by position while globals need a dictionary lookup. Hot loops get noticeably faster.

q: range(1e9) in Python gives…
w: 1e9 is a float literal. Write 10**9. Same trap when sizing lists.

q: list(itertools.accumulate([3, 1, 4], initial=0)) gives…
w: With initial=0, pre[r] − pre[l] is the sum of a[l:r]. initial needs Python 3.8+.

q: A Python dict keyed by ints gets hacked into TLE on Codeforces. Why, and the fix?
o: Crafted keys collide in the hash table; xor each key with a random number
Dicts are always O(n); use lists
The dict is too big; use arrays
w: Anti-hash tests target predictable int hashes. Store key ^ RANDOM, or use sorted arrays with bisect.

q: max([]) in Python…
w: Use max(arr, default=0) or guard the empty case.

q: line = sys.stdin.readline(), and line == "abc" is False even though the input is abc. Why?
o: The input has a byte-order mark
w: int() ignores the trailing newline, string comparison doesn’t. Strip strings you read with readline.

q: collections.Counter("banana").most_common(1) returns…
w: most_common(k) returns a list of (item, count) pairs.

q: In plain Python you need insert, delete and "k-th smallest", 2·10⁵ operations. Usual contest choice?
o: A Fenwick tree over compressed values
w: insort shifts elements, O(n) per insert, which is risky at this size. A BIT over coordinate-compressed values gives O(log n) for all three.

q: On a sorted list, bisect_right(a, x) − bisect_left(a, x) gives…
o: Whether x exists, as a bool
How many elements are less than x
w: Both are O(log n). bisect_left alone gives the count of elements less than x.

q: "Find the minimum x such that check(x) is true", and check is monotonic. Technique?
w: Monotonic means false…false, true…true. Binary search finds the boundary in O(log range) checks.

q: Count subarrays with sum exactly k; values can be negative. Technique?
o: Prefix sums plus a hashmap of counts
w: For each prefix p, add count[p − k]. Two pointers fail with negatives because the window sum isn’t monotonic.

q: All values positive. Longest subarray with sum ≤ S. Technique?
w: With positives, growing the window raises the sum and shrinking lowers it, so each pointer only moves forward. O(n).

q: Shortest path in an unweighted grid. Technique?
w: BFS explores in distance layers in O(V + E). DFS does not give shortest paths.

q: Shortest path, non-negative weights, n up to 2·10⁵. Technique?
w: O((V + E) log V). Bellman–Ford is O(VE) and Floyd–Warshall O(V³), both far too slow here.

q: Edge weights are only 0 or 1. Fastest shortest path?
w: Push 0-weight edges to the front and 1-weight edges to the back. O(V + E).

q: Operations: "merge the groups of a and b" and "are a and b in the same group?" Structure?
w: With path compression, each operation is nearly O(1).

q: Many updates "add v to a[l..r]", then print the final array once. Technique?
w: d[l] += v, d[r + 1] −= v, then one prefix sum at the end: O(n + q). A lazy segment tree is only needed when queries come in between.

q: For each element, find the nearest larger element to its right. Technique?
w: Keep a stack of decreasing values; each element is pushed and popped once. O(n).

q: Maximum of every window of size k. Technique?
w: Keep indices with decreasing values and drop the front when it leaves the window. O(n).

q: Ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps, mod 10⁹ + 7. Technique?
w: "Count the ways" usually means DP. Take the mod at every step.

q: n ≤ 100 items, capacity W ≤ 10⁵, maximize total value. Technique?
w: O(n · W) = 10⁷. Loop capacity downward so each item is used once. Greedy by ratio only works for the fractional version.

q: Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Technique?
o: Sort by end time, take each one that fits
Sort by start time, take each one that fits
w: Finishing earliest leaves the most room. Sorting by start fails on one long early interval.

q: Rules like "a before b"; find a valid order or report a cycle. Technique?
w: Repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0. If fewer than n come out, there is a cycle.

q: Point updates and range sum queries, 2·10⁵ of each. Technique?
w: O(log n) per operation. Prefix sums need an O(n) rebuild after every update.

q: Count pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j], n = 2·10⁵. Technique?
o: Merge sort counting or a Fenwick tree
w: That is inversion counting, O(n log n). The double loop is 2·10¹⁰.

q: Count the separate regions of "#" cells in a grid. Technique?
o: Flood fill (BFS/DFS) from each unvisited cell
w: Each new starting cell is a new region. DSU over cells also works.

q: Two strings of length ≤ 5000; longest common subsequence. Technique?
w: dp[i][j] comes from dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1] and dp[i−1][j−1] + 1. In Python, 2.5·10⁷ steps is risky: keep two rows and use PyPy.

q: Connect all n cities with the minimum total road cost. Technique?
w: Sort edges by cost and take each one that joins two different components. Dijkstra builds a shortest-path tree, a different thing.

q: Can the graph be 2-colored so no edge joins equal colors? Technique?
w: Color the start 0, its neighbors 1, and so on. A conflict means an odd cycle, so not bipartite.

q: n ≤ 15 cities; visit all with minimum cost. Technique?
o: Bitmask DP over (visited set, current city)
w: O(2ⁿ · n²) ≈ 7·10⁶. 15! is about 1.3·10¹², and nearest neighbor isn’t optimal.

q: "Minimize the maximum" or "maximize the minimum" in a statement usually hints at…
w: Guess the bound, then check feasibility, often with a greedy. The check is usually monotonic.

q: XOR of a[l..r] for many queries. Technique?
w: XOR cancels itself, so prefix XOR works exactly like prefix sums.

q: Longest strictly increasing subsequence, n = 2·10⁵. Technique?
o: Tails array with bisect_left: O(n log n)
w: tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. Use bisect_right for non-decreasing.

q: Every operation changes the total sum by an even amount. Start sum is odd, target is even. Conclusion?
w: Look for invariants (parity, sum mod k, sorted order) before simulating. They settle "impossible" cases instantly.

q: For every node of a rooted tree, answer something about its whole subtree. Usual approach?
o: One DFS combining child results bottom-up, or an Euler tour
w: Children finish before parents, so merge their results. An Euler tour turns each subtree into a contiguous range for range queries.

q: Count the primes up to 10⁷. Technique?
o: A Fermat test on each number
w: The sieve is O(N log log N). Trial division on each number is roughly N√N.

q: Static array, many queries "gcd of a[l..r]". Fastest per query?
o: Sparse table: O(1) per query after an O(n log n) build
w: gcd doesn’t care about overlap, like min, so two overlapping blocks answer a query. Prefix gcd can’t be "subtracted" like prefix sums.

q: Find the largest x with ok(x) true. What goes wrong?
o: Infinite loop when hi = lo + 1, because mid rounds down to lo
It returns the smallest such x
w: When the true branch sets lo = mid, round up: mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2.

q: l and r are 1-indexed and inclusive. What’s wrong with ans?
k:
pre = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + a[i]

ans = pre[r] - pre[l]
o: It should be pre[r] − pre[l − 1]; this drops a[l]
w: pre[k] is the sum of the first k elements, so the inclusive range [l, r] is pre[r] − pre[l − 1].

q: This BFS marks visited when popping. Problem?
o: Nodes get queued many times: mark seen when pushing
w: A node can be appended once per neighbor before it is popped, which can TLE and break distance logic. Mark seen[v] right before q.append(v), and mark s at the start.

q: Kadane’s algorithm. Which input gives a wrong answer?
k:
best = 0
cur = 0
for x in a:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)
    best = max(best, cur)
w: The answer should be −2, but best starts at 0. Start best at a[0] (or −infinity) when the subarray must be non-empty.

q: Bug in this sieve?
o: range(i * i, n, i) never reaches n, so n can be wrongly marked prime
w: Use range(i * i, n + 1, i). Starting at i * i is correct and faster than 2 * i.

q: The grid has n rows and m columns, 0-indexed. Bug?
o: The bounds should be < n and < m; this steps one past the edge
w: Valid rows are 0 to n − 1. Python won’t crash on index −1, so the lower bound check matters too.

q: Meant to remove all even numbers. With a = [2, 4, 5], what is a afterward?
w: Removing 2 shifts 4 into the slot the loop already passed. Never mutate a list while iterating it: a = [x for x in a if x % 2].

q: Meant to count pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] = k. Bug?
o: j should start at i + 1; this counts (i, i) and both orders
The loops should go to n + 1
w: Use range(i + 1, n). For large n, switch to a count map.

q: Longest window with sum ≤ S, all values positive. Bug?
o: The while loop never subtracts a[l], so it never ends
w: Inside the loop: s −= a[l], then l += 1. Shrinking a window must undo the element’s contribution.

q: DSU union. Bug?
k:
def union(a, b):
    parent[a] = b
o: It must link the roots: parent[find(a)] = find(b)
w: Linking a non-root overwrites a’s old parent and can split its set. Find both roots, stop if equal, then link.

q: Your teammate ports this to C++ as ans = (a - b) % MOD; with long long. Problem?
k:
MOD = 10**9 + 7
ans = (a - b) % MOD
o: In C++ it can go negative: use ((a − b) % MOD + MOD) % MOD
w: Python’s % is never negative for a positive MOD. C++ keeps the sign of a − b.

q: Dijkstra in Python. What is missing that can cause TLE?
o: if d > dist[u]: continue, to skip stale heap entries
w: Outdated entries still get popped and re-scan all their edges. One line after heappop fixes it.

q: A line "admin" is in the input, but YES never prints. Why?
w: Strip strings read with readline. int() hides this bug for numbers, which is why it surprises people.

q: This "memoized" DP is still exponential. Why?
o: It never stores res in memo
w: Add memo[i] = res before returning. For n = 10⁵ the recursion depth also fails in Python, so write it bottom-up.

q: Building a number mod 10⁹ + 7 from 10⁶ digits in Python. Problem?
k:
ans = 0
for i in range(n):
    ans = ans * 10 + d[i]
ans %= MOD
o: ans grows to a million digits and every step gets slower; take % MOD inside the loop
w: Python won’t overflow, but huge ints make each operation slow. Reduce every step: ans = (ans * 10 + d[i]) % MOD.

q: Iterative DFS with your own stack. What goes in the blank?
w: Mark when pushing, same as BFS, so each node enters the stack once. This replaces recursive DFS and avoids the recursion limit.

q: DSU find with path compression. Fill the blank.
w: Path halving: point x at its grandparent while walking up. Iterative, so no recursion depth issues in Python.

q: Read a grid of n rows of characters. Which line builds it?
k:
n, m = map(int, input().split())
grid = ________
w: One string per row, n rows. grid[r][c] then reads a cell. Strip so a stray "\r" or newline doesn’t become a column.

q: Lower-bound binary search: first index where a[i] >= x (or n). Fill the blank.
w: The half-open [lo, hi) template: keep mid as a candidate with hi = mid, discard it with lo = mid + 1. Memorize this one shape and reuse it everywhere.

q: Build an adjacency list for an undirected graph with nodes 1..n and m edges. Fill the blank.
k:
adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for _ in range(m):
    u, v = map(int, input().split())
    ________
w: Undirected means both directions. Size n + 1 so 1-indexed nodes fit without shifting.

q: BFS distances on a grid. Fill the blank.
w: dist = −1 doubles as "not visited", so you don’t need a separate seen array.

q: Difference array: add v to a[l..r] (0-indexed, inclusive). Fill the blank.
k:
d = [0] * (n + 1)
for l, r, v in updates:
    d[l] += v
    ________
acc = 0
for i in range(n):
    acc += d[i]
    a[i] += acc
w: The effect stops after r, so cancel it at r + 1. That is why d has size n + 1.

q: Count how many times each value appears. Cleanest Python?

q: 0/1 knapsack in one array. Fill the blank.
w: Going downward means dp[c − w] still holds the value before this item, so each item is used once. Going upward gives unbounded knapsack.

q: Bitmask DP over subsets. Which loop order is right for dp[mask | 1 << j] from dp[mask]?

w: Adding a bit makes the number bigger, so increasing mask order already processes every state before it’s used. In Python use PyPy past n ≈ 16.

q: Sum of a[l:r] (0-indexed, r exclusive) with pre[0] = 0 and pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + a[i]. Which expression?
w: Half-open ranges match Python slicing and remove the ±1 bookkeeping. Pick one convention and always use it.
